title: Why blessings come first
hook: a book about farming opens with blessings: thank before you take
tomorrow: The corner of the field (Mishnah Peah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zeraim, and your line: seeds. A harvest that carries other people's shares. Whose share did you notice on your plate? Day one thousand sixty-nine.

What should the first page of a farming law book talk about? Soil, maybe. When to plant. How deep. Which seeds go where. The Mishnah's order of seeds does get to fields and furrows. But its first tractate isn't about soil at all. Before a single furrow is plowed, before anyone talks about corners or tithes or the seventh year, the order of seeds opens with a book called Berakhot. Blessings. Prayer at night and in the morning. Words to say before you bite into bread. A farming book that starts with thank you. Today, why.
screen: `A FARMING BOOK. PAGE ONE?` → `NOT SOIL. BLESSINGS.` → `A FARMING BOOK THAT STARTS WITH THANKS.`

segments.voice: Why blessings come first. Start with what's inside Berakhot. It opens with the Shema, the words said at night and in the morning. Then the standing prayer. Then food: which blessing for the fruit of a tree, which for what grows from the ground, which for bread. And then, near the end, it walks out of the house and into the world. On seeing lightning or hearing thunder, the Mishnah says, a person blesses the one whose strength and might fill the world. On seeing mountains and seas and deserts, the one who makes the work of creation. And then a harder line: a person is to bless over bad news just as over good. So the first tractate isn't only about food. It's about a habit: meeting what comes with words of acknowledgment. Now, why put it at the head of the order about farms? The Mishnah doesn't explain itself, so readers have offered answers. One runs like this: the order of seeds is about what you owe from your harvest, the corner, the tithes, the first fruits. Before you learn what you owe, you learn whose it was to begin with. A companion work to the Mishnah, the Tosefta, puts the principle plainly: a person shouldn't taste anything without first saying a blessing. And it gives the reason with a line from the Psalms, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Thank before you take. In this way of seeing, the blessing isn't decoration on a meal. It's the first act of the harvest.
screen: `SHEMA, PRAYER, THEN FOOD.` · `LIGHTNING, MOUNTAINS, AND BAD NEWS TOO.` · `BEFORE WHAT YOU OWE, WHOSE IT WAS.` · `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · then, large: `THANKS BEFORE THE HARVEST.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: thank before you eat. Bring something to the bell with you, a cup of tea, a piece of fruit, whatever's next. Don't touch it yet. Sit and breathe, and just look at it. Notice the small urge to reach for it, and let it wait. Then let your attention widen past it, the way Berakhot walks out of the house: the light in the room, a sound outside. When the bell ends, before the first bite or sip, if you pray, you can say the blessing your tradition uses. If you don't, say a plain thank you, out loud or inside, to whoever and whatever brought it to you. Then eat. The bell holds the time.
Why blessings come first. The order of seeds opens with Berakhot, so that before you learn what you owe from a harvest, you thank for it. Today's word.
Your line: thanks before the harvest. Today, before you take something good, a meal, a paycheck, a compliment, pause long enough to say thanks first. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews say a blessing before eating and another after, and there are blessings for seeing lightning, mountains or the sea, for good news and for bad; the rules for all of them are set out in tractate Berakhot.

Mishnah Berakhot 9:2 paraphrased: on lightning/thunder, 'whose strength and might fill the world'; on mountains, seas, deserts, 'who makes the work of creation' (the Mishnah lists more). 9:5 paraphrased: bless over bad as over good. Please confirm.
Tosefta Berakhot 4:1 paraphrased: a person should not taste anything until he blesses, citing Psalm 24:1. Please confirm the reference.
Psalm 24:1 quoted from JPS 1917 ('The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof.'). Please confirm.
The reason for Berakhot's placement is given as one reading ('readers have offered answers'), not as the Mishnah's own explanation.
